description: Es un equipo innovador y apasionado por la tecnología, comprometido con transformar ideas en soluciones de impacto. Afrontamos cada desafío con creatividad, entusiasmo y perseverancia, convencidos de que el trabajo en equipo nos permite superar límites, aprender constantemente y alcanzar grandes objetivos. Soñamos en grande, innovamos sin límites y avanzamos juntos hacia nuevas fronteras.
summary:
Nova Core Orbita is a virtual reality game for Meta Quest that puts players inside the International Space Station during a critical power failure. After a short training room and a cinematic intro, the player must find a spare energy module, carry it by hand through the station’s modules, and install it using a robotic arm. Then they suit up, depressurize the airlock, and perform a spacewalk with a thruster backpack to repair a damaged solar panel.

The game responds to Last Light by turning abstract knowledge about life and work in orbit into something people can experience directly. Players learn how the ISS is organized, why power is critical, how an airlock works, and how objects behave in microgravity. They learn by doing, not by reading.

This matters because space exploration often feels distant and inaccessible. Many students will never visit a space center, but a VR headset can bring them inside a realistic station in minutes. By combining guided missions, hands-on interaction and narrative, Nova Core Orbita aims to spark curiosity about science, engineering and space careers, especially among young people.
details:
What it does and how it works

Nova Core Órbita is a first-person VR experience built around a single energy emergency, solved through two missions. The game begins in a closed training room. A dark screen with controller diagrams teaches each mechanic step by step: moving, grabbing, using tools, finding the path and opening hatches. Players who want to go straight to the action can skip the training. When the player crosses the exit hatch, an intro video sets up the story, and it can be skipped. The game then starts.

The station is split into separate, decorated scenes that match the real modules of the 3D model we use:

  • Unity Node 1: the hub that connects the station.
  • Destiny: the laboratory, where the spare power module is stored.
  • Zvezda: the service module, with a robotic control console facing the window.
  • Quest: the airlock, where the spacesuit is prepared.
  • Cupola: the observation module, with Earth and the Moon outside.
  • An exterior EVA scene at real scale, built from the full ISS model.

From outside the station, players can also point at any module and enter it directly.

  • Mission 1 – Power Module Replacement. Mission Control reports an electrical failure. The player activates the emergency protocol and finds the spare module in Destiny. They carry it by hand through the Node to Zvezda and place it in the maintenance hatch. Then they activate the robotic console and steer the arm with a joystick to replace the damaged unit.
  • Mission 2 – Solar Panel Repair (EVA). The player puts on the suit, checks its systems, and pulls a lever to depressurize the airlock. They activate the thruster backpack and fly to a damaged solar panel that is throwing sparks. There they repair it with tools: a pistol-grip drill, a hammer, a ratchet and a sealant gun. Finally they return to the airlock, repressurize it, and confirm from the Cupola that station power is stable.

Key features

  • Two movement systems. Inside the station the player walks naturally, so the experience stays comfortable. Outside, movement uses a thruster backpack inspired by NASA’s SAFER rescue unit. Thrust accelerates the player and momentum is conserved, so you keep drifting until you stabilize. Thrusters and tools use separate buttons, a direct request from our playtesters.
  • Microgravity object physics. Loose objects float, drift and spin. Throwing one keeps it moving in a straight line until it bounces off a wall, with mass-based collisions and very low air drag. This lets players feel Newton’s first law instead of just reading about it.
  • Hands, not controllers. Players see gloved hands whose fingers follow the trigger and grip. The hands have physical colliders: they can press buttons by touching them, push levers, and knock floating objects.
  • Physical interaction. Players grab objects up close or with a pointer. Hatches open by pulling them. Mission items are carried in the player’s hand between modules and placed in their correct slots.
  • Guidance so no one gets lost. An animated arrow path and a floating compass point to the current objective, including which hatch to take when the goal is in another module. If the player hesitates, the game offers a contextual hint.
  • Wrist mission tablet. A tablet on the left wrist shows mission status, the list of objectives, a station power gauge, a countdown timer and messages from Mission Control.
  • Gamification. Players earn points for each objective, plus a speed bonus and a final rank (S, A, B or C). Each module hides a collectible mission patch.
  • Atmosphere. The game has an ambient soundtrack, procedural sound effects, sparks from damaged panels, alarm lighting, an astronaut crewmate outside, and views of Earth and the Moon. The Moon uses a real Apollo 11 photograph.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Accessible space education. Anyone with a standalone headset can explore the ISS interior and exterior, with no specialized facilities needed.
  • Learning by doing. Concepts such as microgravity, inertia, airlocks, spacesuits, robotic arms, solar power and module layout are experienced through action.
  • Inspiration. A short, complete story with clear goals keeps players engaged, and is designed to spark interest in STEM and space careers.
  • Designed for real audiences. The game is meant for science fairs, schools and outreach events. Sessions are short and include an optional tutorial for first-time VR users.

Tools and technologies

  • Engine: Unity 6 with the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), optimized for mobile VR.
    • a public 3D model of the ISS;
    • tool models;
    • an astronaut model that we optimized ourselves (decompressed and rescaled);
    • an Apollo 11 photograph of the Moon.
  • Media: an original cinematic intro video, procedurally generated textures, icons and ambient music, and video re-encoded for Quest playback.
  • Editor tooling: custom Unity editor scripts that generate every module scene automatically. This lets the team rebuild and iterate quickly and consistently.
  • Collaboration: Git with Git LFS for large 3D, texture and video files, and GitHub to coordinate a five-person team.

What makes it creative

  • Instead of a static tour, the ISS becomes the setting for a story. Each module has a purpose in the plot, not just a label.
  • The game combines realistic references (the ISS layout, airlock procedure, SAFER-style thrusters and microgravity behavior) with game design: guidance arrows, hints, scoring and collectibles.
  • Inside and outside are connected. Players can enter any module from the exterior view, and a spacewalk links the two.
  • Mission items are physical objects that players carry and install with their own hands, not menu actions.

Factors the team considered

  • Comfort in VR. Interior movement is smooth walking, turning uses snap turns, the camera never moves without the player’s input, and fades soften every scene change.
    • We added a skippable tutorial, clearer prompts and arrow guidance after testers got lost.
    • We separated the thruster controls from the tool controls.
    • We replaced controllers with hands, and made hatches open by hand.
    • We fixed flickering geometry and corrected the scale of models.
  • Performance on standalone hardware. We used static batching, compressed textures sized for Quest, a reduced camera range and lightweight effects.
  • Scientific honesty. Procedures are simplified for gameplay, and the game does not present them as real NASA training. Physics values are approximations chosen to be believable and educational.
  • Accessibility and audience. Sessions are short, objectives are clear, the experience is in Spanish for our local audience, and the intro is skippable for players who want to go straight to the game.
  • Teamwork and maintainability. Clear module boundaries let five people work in parallel. One person built the wrist tablet and Mission Control messaging, while others worked on missions, environments and VR interaction.
